html:
The prazos were great estates along the Zambezi river in Mozambique, leased by the Portuguese crown from the 17th century to settlers who in practice ruled them as lords.

The holders, called prazeiros, were often of mixed Portuguese, Indian and African descent and married into local families. They collected tribute from the African farmers, traded ivory and gold, and kept private armies of enslaved soldiers called chikunda, who later raided widely for slaves.

By the 19th century some prazo families, such as those of Massangano, were warlords who fought Portugal itself. The system was ended formally in 1930, and much of the land passed to chartered companies. It shaped the valley where the Mutapa state had ruled and where the Cahora Bassa Dam now stands.
sum: The prazos were great estates along the Zambezi river in Mozambique, leased by the Portuguese crown from the 17th century to settlers who in practice ruled them as lords.
